name: Marco Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My brother Lars and I own Høgdal Farm together, but I run it. Six hundred ewes, sixty beef cattle, spring barley, and a small campsite in the top meadow that my wife Sofie looks after in summer. My day starts with the phone: the cattle wear virtual fence collars, so I check where they've grazed overnight, and the AI tells me which paddock to move them to. Then it's out with the dog for the sheep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up with the collars and the AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the one who reads about everything and tries it first. The collars came in three years ago, I was the first in the valley, and half the neighbours laughed. Now four of them have them. I use the AI every day, for grazing, for the campsite bookings, for arguing with the bank about our loan. Lars thinks I'm a gadget man, but he doesn't complain when he doesn't have to fix fences.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a good tool that got oversold, which is true of most tools. I'd say that at the farmers' discussion group, and maybe in a post for the sheep breeders' forum. I'd still recommend the useful bits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means my small head start stays a small head start. The collars and the grazing planner save me maybe ten hours a week. That's worth something, but it doesn't change the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do and look for the next small gain, maybe a drone to count ewes on the hill. Keep paying the farm loan on time and the extra two hundred a month into savings. Probably push the campsite a bit harder with better online booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bored? Why bored?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like the race. When something new works, I get a buzz out of being first. A plateau means the race stops, and farming goes back to being just weather and prices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside to being the gadget man?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money. I've spent maybe eight thousand on things that didn't work. A soil sensor that died after a winter. Sofie keeps the list on the fridge, to remind me.

S0.say: I'd tell the discussion group and the sheep breeders' forum that AI is a good tool that got oversold, like most tools. I'd still recommend the useful bits.
S0.think: My small head start stays small, since the collars and grazing planner save maybe ten hours a week. That's worth something but doesn't change the farm.
S0.do: Looks for the next small gain, such as a drone to count ewes on the hill, and improves online booking for the campsite. Keeps paying the farm loan and adds two hundred a month to savings.
S0.quote: A plateau means the race stops, and farming goes back to being just weather and prices.
S0.fieldNote: Marco gets energy from being first and admits a plateau would bore him. He is candid about the cost of his habit, eight thousand on gadgets that failed. His wife keeping that list on the fridge says a lot about how the household balances him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for farms that move early. I'd say it at the discussion group and offer to show people what I'm using. It's a business change, like when tractors came in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me, because I own the land with Lars and I already know the tools. The farms that'll struggle are the ones that wait. Some of them are my friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd buy a small robot for the barley weeding and look at an automatic feeder for the cattle in winter. That's maybe forty thousand, which means a bigger loan, but with fixed interest. I'd also try selling our lamb straight to customers online, because the AI would handle most of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bigger loan. With one to six months saved, isn't that a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is. Sofie would say so, and she'd be right to. I'd only do it if the bank gave us a two-year payment holiday on it and the numbers worked with a bad lamb price, not a good one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which friends would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Erling down the road, who still bales small bales by hand and refuses to own a smartphone. I'd offer to help him. He'd say no, and then I'd do it anyway, probably.

S1.say: I'd tell the discussion group this is good news for farms that move early, and offer to show people what I use. It's a business change, like when tractors came in.
S1.think: It's good for me because Lars and I own the land and I already know the tools. The farms that wait will struggle, and some of them belong to friends.
S1.do: Buys a small weeding robot for the barley and looks at an automatic winter feeder, about forty thousand on a fixed-rate loan, only if the bank gives a payment holiday and it works at a bad lamb price. Starts selling lamb direct online.
S1.quote: I'd only do it if the bank gave us a two-year payment holiday on it and the numbers worked with a bad lamb price, not a good one.
S1.fieldNote: Marco is a cautious risk-taker: keen to borrow and buy, but testing the numbers against a bad year. He frames the change as ordinary business history. He thinks of a neighbour who refuses to change and plans to help him whether he likes it or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming too fast for small farms to keep up, and the big operators with cash will win. I'd say the government should help small farms buy in, maybe cheap loans. I'd say it plainly, not angrily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried. Being early only helps if you've got time to use it. In two years, the big farm companies would have whole fleets, and they'd produce lamb and barley cheaper than me. And our campsite needs people with jobs and holiday money, and if lots of people lose work, who's camping?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd lease robots rather than buy them, so I'm not stuck with old kit in a year. I'd fix the loan rate and cut the extras, no new pickup, no holiday. Then I'd talk to three other family farms about sharing a robot fleet and selling together, because alone we're too small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. My mind's running faster than the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said lease rather than buy. Why does two years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because in two years the machines will change every six months. Anything I buy is out of date before it's paid off. With more time I'd buy. With two years, I'd rent everything and keep my cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this picture you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not being up at lambing every night for six weeks. I'd welcome that. But I'd welcome it more if I knew the farm would still be ours at the end of it.

S2.say: I'd say plainly that it's too fast for small farms and the big operators with cash will win. The government should help small farms buy in, perhaps with cheap loans.
S2.think: Being early only helps if there's time to use it, and in two years big companies would have whole fleets and undercut me. The campsite also needs people with jobs and holiday money.
S2.do: Leases robots rather than buying, fixes the loan rate and drops extras like a new pickup and holiday. Talks to three other family farms about sharing a robot fleet and selling together.
S2.feel: Anxious, with his mind running faster than the money.
S2.quote: Being early only helps if you've got time to use it.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most tech-keen farmer in the valley is anxious in the fastest picture, because scale and cash beat early adoption. His instinct to lease and pool with neighbours is practical. He spotted a second risk most farmers wouldn't, that the campsite depends on other people's jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for family farms to team up and get ready. I'd say it at the discussion group and offer to organise it. I'd keep it upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is the sweet spot for me. I'm far enough ahead to set it up, and there's time for the prices of robots to drop. I'd be uneasy about the campsite, but the farm side I think I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd get the four-farm group going, with a shared robot for weeding and one for the sheep checks. I'd learn the maintenance myself, online, because I don't want to wait for a dealer. By year three I'd be selling all our lamb direct, with the AI doing the orders, and Sofie would turn the campsite into farm stays with a cooking class.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the way you are before a busy season, not before a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farm stays. Isn't that just as exposed if people lose their jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, fair point. I'd hope the people who keep their money want something real. But I don't know. It's a bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Nils and Ella?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nils is twelve and already fixes the collars with me. I'd tell him to learn how the machines think. Ella wants to run the campsite, so I'd tell her to learn to cook, because people will always want a meal made by someone.

S3.say: I'd tell the discussion group that five years is enough for family farms to team up and get ready, and offer to organise it. I'd keep it upbeat.
S3.think: Five years is the sweet spot, since I'm ahead enough to set things up and robot prices have time to fall. The campsite worries me more than the farm.
S3.do: Sets up a four-farm group with shared robots for weeding and sheep checks, learns robot maintenance online, and moves all lamb sales direct with AI handling orders by year three. Turns the campsite into farm stays with cooking classes with Sofie.
S3.feel: Uneasy, like before a busy season rather than a storm.
S3.quote: Ella wants to run the campsite, so I'd tell her to learn to cook, because people will always want a meal made by someone.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits Marco's style, giving him time to lead rather than scramble. He accepted that his farm-stay idea carries the same risk as the campsite and called it a bet. His son already works on the collars with him, which shapes his advice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for any farm that wants to stay. Learn it, share it, and don't wait for someone to save you. That's what I'd tell anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine, and more than fine. With ten years, the robots get cheaper, I'm already set up, and Lars and I still own the land. The question is whether the land is worth anything when anyone with a robot can farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, adding one machine a year as they prove out. I'd keep saving and pay the loan down faster. I'd put money into Nils's and Ella's education, but I wouldn't tell them what to study yet, because I don't know what will matter in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. This one feels like normal life, just faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You raised whether land will be worth anything. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. Land has always been the safe thing, and Lars and I hold it partly for our kids. If robots make food cheap and plenty of land comes up for sale, prices could drop. I'd keep farming it either way, but I'd feel poorer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The walk with the dog in the morning, if I'm honest. I'd still do it, robots or not. Nobody's taking that.

S4.say: I'd tell anyone that ten years is plenty of time for a farm that wants to stay. Learn it, share it, and don't wait for someone to save you.
S4.think: I'd be more than fine, with robots getting cheaper and the land still ours. The real question is whether the land is worth much when anyone with a robot can farm.
S4.do: Adds one proven machine a year, keeps saving and pays the loan down faster. Sets money aside for both children's education without steering their subjects.
S4.feel: Calm, as if it's normal life only faster.
S4.quote: The walk with the dog in the morning, if I'm honest. I'd still do it, robots or not. Nobody's taking that.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Marco is confident and businesslike. His one real worry was land value, since the land is his family's long-term security. The morning walk with the dog is what he'd keep no matter what.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the big operators would beat us on scale before we could team up. What would help is cheap loans or grants for small family farms to buy or share robots, and some rule that stops a few big companies buying up everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether people would still want food from a real farm with a real face. That's my bet for the next twenty years. I'd love to know if I'm right.

headlineQuote: Our campsite needs people with jobs and holiday money, and if lots of people lose work, who's camping?
portrait: Marco Hansen is 43 and runs Høgdal Farm, which he owns with his brother Lars: six hundred ewes, sixty cattle on virtual fence collars, spring barley and a summer campsite run by his wife Sofie. He uses AI every day and loves being first, though he admits to eight thousand spent on gadgets that failed. He is calm and even excited through the plateau and steady change, but anxious about two-year AGI, when big operators with fleets would undercut him and fewer people could afford holidays. With five or ten years he plans a shared robot group with neighbouring farms, direct lamb sales and farm stays, and his main lingering worry is what the land will be worth.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because large operators would beat family farms on scale before they could team up.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap loans or grants for family farms to buy or share robots, and rules that stop a few big companies buying up everything.
